newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian sugar would gain from Belarus integration.
newsitem.headline: Russian sugar would gain from Belarus integration.

text.p: A merger between Russia and Belarus would help stem the flow of Ukrainian white sugar smuggled into Russia, bringing some relief to Russian refiners, sugar traders said on Friday.

Russia's refineries complain that they cannot compete with cheap imports of Ukrainian white sugar, especially that smuggled through Belarus, which is not subject to a 10 percent import duty levied on sugar brought from Ukraine.
"Yes, the joining of these two countries could definitely help the sugar refining industry in Russia," said one senior Moscow-based sugar dealer.
President Boris Yeltsin, quoted by Interfax news agency, said earlier on Friday that Russia and Belarus could merge in the future, though he did not give a time frame for such a move.
The two former Soviet republics have already announced plans to seek closer ties, although Moscow has been cautious about how far integration might go.
But traders said quantities of whites imported into Russia via Belarus were relatively small and the impact from stricter control over Belarus' leaky border with Ukraine was likely to be limited.
"I don't think we are talking about critical volumes here," said one trader.
He said the practice of smuggling was made possible by a leaky border between Ukraine and Belarus, from which whites could be imported tax-free to Russia.
"The border between Ukraine and Russia is guarded much more carefully," he said.
Russia says Ukraine sugar plants have an unfair advantage over Russian plants because they do not pay value-added tax.
A Foreign Trade Ministry group in August last year called for quotas on white sugar imports of 1.5 million tonnes overall in 1997, with Ukrainian deliveries capped at 1.15 million.
But the government has so far failed to act on the proposal, casting doubts over whether curbs will be implemented.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha said last week that he was confident restrictions would eventually be imposed.
But trade sources in Moscow said government officials were discussing the possibility of raising duties rather than imposing quotas.
"We hear from reliable sources that the talk now is not of quotas but of duties on imports," a trader said.
Ukraine officials say they have the potential to export up to 1.5 million tonnes of whites annually, and that the proposed Russian quotas would hurt the sugar industry.
Russia imported 1.44 tonnes of whites in total in 1996, down from 1.78 million in 1995.
